title: The Role of the State
notes:
THE ARGUMENT OF THE SLIDE

Four problems explain why the state is involved in infrastructure at all, and each calls for a different instrument. The four are chosen because each has an academic source, which is what the week's brief asked for; the familiar list of externalities and public goods is left to the cohorts' own economics modules, and is not used here because I have no paper for it that is specific to infrastructure.

Natural monopoly: Joskow (2005) defines it technologically as a cost function that is subadditive, so one firm supplying output Q costs less than two or more firms splitting it (working-paper page 8). Sunk costs: Joskow's section on sunk costs (pages 20 to 31) argues that sunk cost is the attribute that explains why one or very few firms survive and why the regulator can later be tempted to hold the firm up (pages 20 to 21 and 119). Incomplete contracts: Shleifer (1998), pages 8 to 9, describes the incomplete-contracts idea that ownership gives control where contracts are silent, and that the choice between public and private provision depends on incentives to deliver non-contractible quality; this is the idea Hart (2003) builds on in the focus part. Asymmetric information: the firm knows more than the regulator about its cost opportunities and effort (Joskow, pages 93 to 94 and 119).

SOURCES

Joskow, P. L. (2005), Regulation of Natural Monopolies, MIT Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research Working Paper 05-008, a draft of the chapter published in Polinsky and Shavell (eds) (2007), Handbook of Law and Economics, volume 2, Elsevier (chapter pages 1227 to 1348). Page numbers are those of the 2005 draft (printed page = PDF page minus five). Shleifer, A. (1998), State versus private ownership, Journal of Economic Perspectives 12(4), 133 to 150; I read the NBER working paper version 6665 (printed page = PDF page minus three), so page numbers differ from the journal.

TEACHING POINT

Ask each cohort which of the four it meets first in its own core: Environmental Policy meets the information problem in regulation, Planning meets the sunk-cost and commitment problem in consenting, Real Estate Finance meets incomplete contracts in lease and development agreements. Then say that the rest of the week is about what a state does about each.

title: Natural Monopoly: Subadditive Costs
notes:
THE FIGURE

The curve is average cost for a firm with the cost function C(q) = F + cq, the example Joskow uses (working-paper page 9): a fixed cost F and a constant marginal cost c, so average cost F/q + c falls continuously as output grows. I set F = 500 and c = 2 for illustration; these are not data. One firm supplying 100 units costs 500 + 200 = 700, or 7 a unit. Two firms supplying 50 each cost 2 x (500 + 100) = 1,200, or 12 a unit. The single firm is cheaper, which is what subadditivity means.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Definition (page 8): a natural monopoly exists at output Q when C(Q) is less than the sum of the costs of splitting Q among two or more firms. Scale economies are sufficient for subadditivity but not necessary. Joskow's own example (pages 10 to 11) shows a cost function that has already left the range of economies of scale and is still subadditive, because demand is too small to support two efficient firms; Bonbright (1961) and Posner (1969) are cited on page 17 for network effects that can have the same result. Sunk costs (pages 20 to 21): the most important attribute missing from the textbook definition. Where the fixed cost is sunk, a monopoly is both more likely to emerge and harder to discipline by threat of entry, and the firm is exposed to holdup after it has invested.

Last line of the slide: a monopoly can be cheaper to run and costlier to use. Joskow's Figure 5A compares a second-best price that just covers cost with the unregulated outcome (page 34); the case for regulation rests on the gap between the two (page 20, 'foundation for arguments for introducing price and entry regulation').

SOURCE

Joskow (2005), working-paper pages 8 to 11, 17, 20 to 21 and 34 (printed pages; PDF page minus five). The empirical evidence for subadditivity is thin: Joskow, page 31, says there is surprisingly little work that measures it, mostly for electricity (Christensen and Green 1976). Say so if a student asks whether water or rail track is a natural monopoly: the claim is plausible and rarely tested.

title: Public Ownership, Franchising or Regulation
notes:
THE THREE RESPONSES

Joskow's overview of regulatory institutions (pages 61 to 69) separates what a government can do about a natural monopoly. It can own the supplier, which Joskow sets aside (page 64: 'I will not cover public enterprise or privatization in this essay'); Shleifer (1998) supplies that case. It can award a franchise by competitive bidding, Demsetz's (1968) 'competition for the market' (Joskow pages 64 to 66). Or it can regulate a private supplier's prices (pages 93 onwards).

Public ownership. Shleifer, pages 8 to 9: ownership gives the owner control where the contract is silent, so a manager who is not the owner has weak incentives to cut costs or to innovate. The argument in favour of state ownership, page 11, is the one Hart, Shleifer and Vishny (1997) make for prisons: where cost cutting damages quality that cannot be contracted on, soft incentives may be better, 'to avoid untrained low-wage guards'. Shleifer's own conclusion is that even there private ownership is usually superior, once competition, reputation and not-for-profit provision are considered (pages 11 to 14); and on corruption the argument is ambiguous (page 17). The prisons case is where the argument about quality is strongest, and the one Hart uses in the focus part.

Franchise bidding. Joskow, pages 64 to 66: competition at the award stage replaces regulation afterwards, because the contract embodies the terms the auction produced. It needs an adequate number of independent bidders; an optimal auction converges to a fixed-price contract as bidders increase (Laffont and Tirole 1993, p. 318, as cited by Joskow, page 66). Joskow says it fits services whose attributes are easily defined and whose assets are mobile (refuse collection, ambulance services, page 66), not a water network. The weakness is the contract: it is incomplete, which is why Guasch's evidence on renegotiation (part six) matters.

Regulation. Joskow, pages 93 to 94: the regulator is less well informed than the firm, so the process is built around getting better information and using it. The next two slides take this up.

SOURCES

Joskow (2005), pages 61 to 69 and 93 to 94; Shleifer (1998), NBER Working Paper 6665, pages 8 to 9, 11 and 17; Demsetz, H. (1968), Why regulate utilities?, Journal of Law and Economics 11(1), 55 to 65, as cited by Joskow (not read). Hart, O., Shleifer, A. and Vishny, R. W. (1997), The proper scope of government: theory and an application to prisons, Quarterly Journal of Economics 112(4), 1127 to 1161, as cited by Shleifer and by Hart (not read).

title: Data Centres and the Local Economy
notes:
WHY THIS SLIDE IS HERE

Data centres run through the whole course as the hot example, with one aspect each week. In Week 2 the aspect is who gains and who pays when a large, concentrated load arrives, and which part of the state decides. The slide sits in the part on the role of the state because it is a case of externalities, incidence and the choice of instrument. Week 1 took the scale of the buildout, Week 3 takes how it is financed, and Week 7 takes the ESG questions.

THE FIGURE

Alvarez, Argente, Chow and Van Patten (2026), Data Centers and Local Economies in the Age of AI: A Shift-Share Approach, NBER Working Paper 35194, May 2026, revised September 2026. The authors link a facility-level panel of US data centres (the 451 Research Datacenter Knowledge Base, S&P Global) to county outcomes. Because sites are not chosen at random, they instrument local development with historical corridor geography: terrain-based routes from the 1855 Pacific railroad survey, interacted with 1870 rail coverage and the orientation of access nodes, and with growth in scale-oriented facilities outside the United States (abstract; pages 2 to 3). In the 1995 to 2023 long-difference specification, a 10 per cent increase in cumulative annualised data-centre revenue raises total employment by 2.7 per cent, construction employment by 6.0, establishments by 2.3, payroll by 3.6 and electricity prices by 0.5 per cent, with an additional 4.4 percentage points of house-price growth (pages 3 to 4). At the latest endpoints the paper reports tax returns up 1.1 per cent, adjusted gross income 2.3 and wages 1.9 through 2022, and public-supply water withdrawals up 3.1 per cent through 2020 (page 4). The slide shows the first six. In the pooled shift-share design the house price and electricity price estimates are positive but less precisely estimated (page 3), so say that the price effects are the less certain half of the picture.

THE WHOLESALE MARKET

Kay, Reaser and Taylor (2026), Processing Power: The Effect of Data Centers on Wholesale Electricity Markets, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas Working Paper 2606, March 2026, revised October 2026 (abstract, page 1). With an hourly dispatch model of 23 regional markets, they estimate that data centres raised wholesale prices by 6.9 per cent nationally by 2025 and by 15.0 per cent in northern Virginia, and that under their preferred scenario the national effect reaches 12.3 per cent by 2028. Roughly half of the increase in generator payments is a transfer to inframarginal generators. They also derive sufficient statistics for when load growth lowers retail rates, because fixed network costs are spread over more kilowatt-hours while higher-cost plants set the margin (page 1). So the sign of the retail effect is ambiguous, and the paper's contribution is to say what it depends on.

HOW IT LINKS TO THE LECTURE

The county gains jobs and tax base, and the grid and water system carry the load. The consent decision is local, the grid cost is regional or national, and the carbon cost is global, so no single authority sees the whole bill. This is the externality and public goods material of the first slides of the week, and it is what the Heathrow case asks students to apply to an airport. Kay and co-authors' point about transfers is a point about who captures the rent when a regulator or market sets the price of scarce capacity.

CAUTIONS

Both papers are working papers and not peer reviewed, and both study US counties and markets. Evidence on house prices conflicts: another study, seen here only as a search listing and not read, finds that the announcement of a large data centre lowers house values within three miles by about 3 per cent, and a Yue and Zeng working paper (SSRN) reports local employment and electricity price effects with a different design. Treat the direction of the house-price effect as unsettled and say so.

QUESTIONS FOR THE ROOM

Which of the gains in the figure accrue to the county that decides, and which of the pressures fall on people who do not? What instrument would you use to make the connecting user pay for the network it needs, and who should decide it?

title: National Totals and Local Constraints: Water and the Grid
notes:
WHY THIS SLIDE IS HERE

This is the second data-centre slide of the week and it makes a methodological point that the other cohorts need as much as the planners: a national aggregate can be reported honestly and still answer the wrong question, because an infrastructure load arrives at one place and meets one local system. It sits in the part on the role of the state, next to the slide on local gains and costs, and it prepares the later parts on public investment management (appraisal needs the local unit of analysis) and on regulation of the grid.

THE LEFT PANEL: WATER IN ENGLAND

All numbers are verified in Resources/Week 2/RE07 Reality Check - AI infrastructure/Source verification.md, from the Environment Agency's 2024 to 2025 water resources report and the WRc and MOSL report Water Efficient Data Centres (February 2026). In million litres a day: household 8,200, other non-household 2,725, leaks 2,617 (the Environment Agency's figure, described as the lowest in two decades and 19 per cent of treated water), data centres 5.15, from 1,879,000 cubic metres a year for England. Leakage is about 508 times data-centre use. The bars are on a logarithmic scale because on a linear scale the data centre bar is a sliver and the ratio cannot be read; the broadcast graphic in the programme used a linear scale and mislabelled the area, which is recorded in the verification note. The household figure of 8,200 is as given on the programme and is consistent with Environment Agency reporting, not independently recomputed.

THE CONCENTRATION THE AGGREGATE HIDES

The WRc and MOSL report surveyed 257 English data centres (1,066,000 cubic metres a year, scaled to 1,879,000 for England). Sixty-seven per cent use less than 1,000 cubic metres a year, a mean of 217, comparable to a 600 square metre office. The six largest, 3 per cent of the sample, each use more than 50,000 cubic metres, average 115,800 (comparable to a hospital of 37,000 square metres) and account for 65 per cent of the sector's water; the largest fifteen account for over 80 per cent. Two of the six came online in 2024 and five since 2020. A small water resource zone such as Henley in the Thames Water area supplies about 5,000,000 cubic metres a year, which is the scale at which a single large facility would matter.

THE RIGHT PANEL: THE GRID

Ofgem identified around 140 data-centre projects seeking connection, about 50 GW, earlier in 2026. By the end of July 2026 applications from large electricity users had reached 125 GW, up from 41 GW in under a year, with at least 80 GW from data centres, against a peak demand of about 58 GW in 2023 (figures as stated on the Spectator's Reality Check programme, recorded in August 2026, and checked there against Ofgem's connection reform material; I have not seen the Ofgem release itself, and the programme gives the peak demand as a winter peak of the right order). A connection queue is a register of options and not a forecast. The presenter says that many applications are speculative and that the 80 GW will not run at once, which is the right caveat.

THE ACADEMIC ANCHOR

Li, Yang, Islam and Ren (2025), Making AI Less Thirsty, Communications of the ACM, DOI 10.1145/3724499 (pages 1 to 8 of the author copy; check the volume and page numbers in the journal). The paper separates scope-1 water used on site for cooling from scope-2 water used to generate the electricity, and shows that water efficiency varies by place and by hour because it depends on weather and on the grid's fuel mix (page 7). Its projection is that the global AI demand could account for 4.2 to 6.6 billion cubic metres of water withdrawal in 2027, with 0.38 to 0.60 billion cubic metres evaporated and counted as consumption (page 1). The global figure sounds large and says little about any one catchment, which is the point of the slide. The paper's own recommendation is increased transparency and reporting of the water footprint (page 8). Alvarez and co-authors find public-supply water withdrawals up 3.1 per cent through 2020 for a 10 per cent rise in data-centre revenue, which is a US county result and not an English one.

THE LESSON

At 19:23 of the programme the presenter turns his own finding against itself: national water use is a rounding error, but a large facility appears in one place and draws on one local system. The general proposition is that aggregation destroys the information that determines whether a project is feasible. It extends to network capacity, labour markets and construction supply chains. For appraisal, the unit of analysis is the local system, which is why the consent regime and the connection regime are local and regional institutions.

WHO PAYS FOR THE NETWORK

The American response described in the programme is the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, signed in March 2026, under which major operators undertake to fund their own connection infrastructure and not to socialise it through consumer bills (confirmed as described in the verification note). Britain has not yet had to settle the question, and the Heathrow case in the second hour raises the same question for an airport.

QUESTIONS FOR THE ROOM

What is the right denominator for a water statistic about a facility? If connection applications are options and not demand, how should a system operator ration capacity, and who should pay for reinforcement ahead of demand? How would you design a connection charge that makes the speculative applicants pay for the option?

title: Public Investment Management
notes:
THE FIGURE AND ITS SOURCE

Dabla-Norris, Brumby, Kyobe, Mills and Papageorgiou (2011), IMF Working Paper 11/37, build an index of the institutions behind public investment, scoring 71 countries (40 of them low-income) on four stages, each from 0 to 4: project appraisal, selection, implementation and evaluation (abstract, and pages 7 to 12 for the components). The figure plots the four sub-index means reported on pages 15 to 17: appraisal 1.49 (standard deviation 1.09, with nine countries scoring zero and South Africa and Colombia the maximum of 4, and 25 countries scoring 1 or lower; page 16), selection 1.89 (standard deviation 0.77; page 17), implementation 1.97 (page 17) and evaluation 1.42 (page 17). The mean of the overall index is 1.68 (standard deviation 0.66; page 15), which is the mean of the four, to rounding.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Appraisal and evaluation are weak in every region (page 17). The top five are middle-income (South Africa, Brazil, Colombia, Tunisia, Thailand); the bottom five are largely low-income (Belize, Congo Republic, Solomon Islands, Yemen, West Bank and Gaza) (page 15). Income is not destiny: Bolivia and Rwanda score above 2 and exceed 19 middle-income countries (page 15). Middle- and low-income countries score about the same on implementation, and differ most on appraisal, selection and evaluation (page 16).

Why the index matters for the week: investment spending is a poor proxy for the accumulation of productive assets where there is waste or corruption (pages 5 to 6), and the paper cites Pritchett (2000) for the gap between what an investment costs and the capital value it creates. This is the Week 1 argument about selection in institutional form. Caveats the paper states (page 12 and later): the index measures the institutional setting and not performance, and its link to growth is left for further work.

SOURCE

Dabla-Norris, E., Brumby, J., Kyobe, A., Mills, Z. and Papageorgiou, C. (2011), Investing in public investment: an index of public investment efficiency, IMF Working Paper WP/11/37; published as Journal of Economic Growth 17(3), 2012, 235 to 266 (the search record I saw confirms the abstract, not the page content). Page numbers are those of the working paper (printed page = PDF page minus one). The paper's data are survey-based and the authors acknowledge the index is not replicable from public data, a point a later critique makes.

title: PIMA: Design Outruns Effectiveness
notes:
THE FIGURE

The chart is from the IMF's launch presentation for Well Spent (Verdier, 'Strong Infrastructure Governance for Strong Recovery', 2 October 2020, slide 5, released by the IMF under a CC0 licence), cropped to the chart. It shows scores for the 15 institutions of the Public Investment Management Assessment, coloured by stage: planning (red), allocation (blue) and implementation (green). On the scale of the chart, which runs from 1.0 to 3.0, the strongest institution is budget comprehensiveness and unity, just under 2.0, and the weakest is project selection, at about 1.3, with project appraisal and the monitoring of public assets next, at about 1.4. I read the values off the chart; the IMF's slide does not print them, so quote them as approximate.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Slide 5 of the presentation: PIMA is designed to assess infrastructure governance institutions; the design of public investment management institutions is generally stronger than the implementation of those systems; effectiveness is low at all stages (planning, allocation and implementation); and it can be improved across all income groups. Slide 4: on average, better infrastructure governance could make up more than half of observed efficiency losses. The book behind it is Schwartz, Fouad, Hansen and Verdier (eds) (2020), Well Spent: How Strong Infrastructure Governance Can End Waste in Public Investment, International Monetary Fund; I have the launch slides but not the book, so the headline efficiency-loss figure (often quoted as about one third) is not on the slide, and should be checked in the book (chapter 4, as the slides cite it) before it is used.

The link to the previous slide: the academic index and the IMF's practitioner tool agree that appraisal and selection are the weak institutions, and that the paper design is stronger than the practice.

SOURCES

title: Cost-of-Service Regulation and Price Caps
notes:
THE FORMULA

Joskow, page 98: the regulated firm's revenue requirement in year t is R(t) = OC(t) + D(t) + s x (1 + tax rate) x RAV(t) + F(t), where OC is operating cost, D depreciation of the regulatory asset base RAV, s the allowed rate of return on the base, and F other costs such as property taxes and franchise fees. This is the 'building block' structure, and the regulatory asset base is what investors in a regulated network buy (Week 1, Thames Water). The rate case sets the revenue requirement first and the tariff structure second (page 97).

COST-OF-SERVICE IN PRACTICE

Joskow, pages 93 to 99: regulators respond to the information problem with a uniform system of accounts, audits, the power to disallow costs they judge unreasonable, and benchmarking against comparable firms ('yardstick' comparisons, page 99). Prices are not adjusted continuously: there are long periods of regulatory lag, during which the firm keeps part of any saving (pages 96 to 97). Averch and Johnson (1962), modelled on pages 113 to 115, show that a firm allowed a return on capital above its cost of capital has an incentive to use too much capital (page 121).

PRICE CAPS AND SLIDING SCALES

Joskow, pages 119 to 128 and 126 to 127: the more recent literature offers a spectrum between cost-of-service, where the price tracks realised cost and the firm has no incentive to cut it, and a fixed price, which gives the firm every incentive but extracts no rent. The optimum lies in between, as a profit-sharing contract or sliding scale (page 126), and a menu of such contracts can do better still (Laffont and Tirole 1993). Price caps have a classic weakness: the firm can raise profit by cutting quality (page 128). In practice, incentive regulation is often added to cost-of-service and not substituted for it (page 94).

CAUTION

Joskow writes about United States commission regulation. The United Kingdom's price-control system, on which the Week 1 slides on Thames Water and Ofwat rest, is a close relative (an allowed return on a regulatory asset base, reset periodically), but I have not cited a primary source on Ofwat's current method; my attempt to retrieve the Ofwat price review documents timed out.

SOURCE

Joskow (2005), working-paper pages 93 to 99, 113 to 115, 119 to 128. Averch, H. and Johnson, L. L. (1962), Behavior of the firm under regulatory constraint, American Economic Review 52(5), 1052 to 1069, as cited by Joskow (not read).

title: Regulatory Design and Renegotiation
notes:
THE FIGURE

Guasch (2004), Granting and Renegotiating Infrastructure Concessions: Doing It Right (World Bank Institute), Table 1.16, printed page 17: the incidence of renegotiation by contract and regulatory feature, in per cent, for a dataset of more than 1,000 concessions granted in Latin America and the Caribbean from 1985 to 2000 (page 12). Where a regulatory body existed, 17 per cent of concessions were renegotiated; where there was none, 61 per cent. Price-cap regulation, 42 per cent; rate-of-return regulation, 13 per cent. Where the regulatory framework was embedded in law, 17 per cent; in a decree, 28 per cent; in the contract itself, 40 per cent (page 16 describes the table).

READING IT

The figures are incidences from simple tabulations ('author's calculations'), not estimates with controls, so they show association and not cause; the book's later chapters estimate the determinants more carefully (I did not read them). The price-cap result is the one to tease out: price caps shift cost risk to the operator, and Guasch's explanation (page 15) is that this raises the operator's incentive to ask for a renegotiation, which is why operators initiated 83 per cent of renegotiations under a price cap against 26 per cent under rate of return (Table 1.14, page 16; see slide 25). The regulator result connects to Joskow: the commitment problem is worse where nobody is in a position to give the firm credible assurance, and where the rules sit in a contract the parties can reopen, as against a law.

Guasch defines renegotiation as a significant change to a concession contract, not envisioned or driven by stated contingencies, in tariffs, investment plans, exclusivity, guarantees, fees, coverage targets, service standards or the concession period; scheduled tariff reviews do not count (page 12).

SOURCE

Guasch, J. L. (2004), Granting and Renegotiating Infrastructure Concessions: Doing It Right, World Bank Institute Development Studies, Washington DC. title: Capture, Ratchets and Hold-up
notes:
THE FOUR PROBLEMS

Each row is a failure Joskow identifies and the institution that has grown up to meet it.

Information gap: the regulated firm knows more about its cost opportunities, demand and managerial effort than the regulator, and has an incentive to use the advantage strategically (pages 93 to 94 and 119). The responses are the uniform system of accounts, audits, the power to disallow costs, third-party participation in rate cases and benchmarking (pages 95 to 99 and 119 to 120).

Capture: if the firm, or another interest group, can capture the regulator, decisions drift towards its interest (page 119, citing Posner 1974, Spiller 1990 and Laffont and Tirole 1993, ch. 5). The responses are transparency requirements, public hearings and written decisions, rules on private communications, appeals court review and legislative oversight (page 120).

Ratchet effects: if the regulator sets price from realised cost, the firm anticipates that any cost saving it reveals will be taken at the next review, so it has less reason to make it (page 146, citing Weitzman 1980). Regulatory lag, in which price is fixed between reviews, and profit sharing are the usual responses (pages 96 and 126).

Hold-up: where investments are long-lived and sunk, other groups can capture the regulator and expropriate the firm's assets after it has invested (page 119). In the United States constitutional protection against taking property without just compensation conditions what a regulator can do (page 61). Outside the United States the commitment has to be made in other ways, which is the point of the earlier slide on rules embedded in law, decree or contract, and of the focus part.

LINK TO THE NEXT PART

Hold-up and ratchets are the same problem seen from the two sides of a concession contract: the operator fears the government will change the terms after the asset is sunk, and the government fears the operator will ask to change them once it is.

title: Delivery Models and the PPP Framework
notes:
THE FOCUS OF THE WEEK

There is a large literature on public-private partnerships, and the aim of this part is not to survey it but to give three clearly different ways of thinking about what a partnership is for, each tied to a paper that can be read in an evening, and each with a page in Lecture Notes/Week 2/web that lets students vary its assumptions. The three are chosen because they disagree about what a partnership is: a bundle of tasks (Hart), a way of sharing demand risk (Engel, Fischer and Galetovic), or a way of raising money (the financing argument, tested by the National Audit Office). The fourth item is the framework a government builds around any of them, measured across 20 European countries by Verhoest and co-authors.

ORDER

First the spectrum, so students can place a project on it (Guasch 2004, Table 2.1). Then each model, as a pair of slides: the paper, then an interactive output. Then the framework. The part closes on a table that compares the three models on what each explains, what it predicts and how it fares against the evidence. The part ends where the following part, on renegotiation, begins: the evidence that contracts are reopened.

READING FOR THE PART

Required: Hart (2003) and Engel, Fischer and Galetovic (2013), as in the reading list. Supporting: National Audit Office (2018), PFI and PF2; Guasch (2004), chapters 1 and 2.

ON HELEN'S OWN WORK

Helen mentioned a review paper of her own that might be cited here. She has since sent 'From participation to partnership' (Environmental Impact Assessment Review, 2026) and said it is relevant but not closely, and that citing it may not be a good idea, so it is not cited. This note records that the question was settled on 2026-10-25.

title: The Delivery Spectrum
notes:
THE TABLE

Guasch (2004), Table 2.1, printed page 25: the jurisdictions and responsibilities under three types of private participation. Under a management contract the government owns the assets, makes the investment, controls service and tariffs, and bears revenue, cost and labour risk; the private operator takes only the risk of its own management cost. Under a concession the private operator makes the investment and bears revenue, cost and labour risk, while ownership stays with the government and control of service and tariffs is shared. Under privatisation the private operator owns the physical and land assets as well. I omitted the row on ownership of vehicles, which is ambiguous in the extracted text of the table.

THE SPECTRUM BETWEEN

Figure 2.1 (page 24) lists the types between public supply and operation and private supply and operation: outsourcing; corporatisation and performance agreements; management contracts; leasing (affermage); franchise; concession; build-operate-transfer (BOT); build-own-operate (BOO); divestiture by licence; divestiture by sale. Guasch says each type differs in government participation, risk allocation, investment responsibilities, operational requirements and operators' incentives (page 23). The most common types are privatisations and concessions, and management contracts much less so (page 23); in Latin America and the Caribbean from 1990 to 2000, concessions were 89 per cent of private-participation projects in water and sanitation, 98 per cent in transport, 54 per cent in energy and 3 per cent in telecommunications (Table 2.2, page 25, from the World Bank's Private Participation in Infrastructure database), because telecoms were divested outright.

Guasch describes a concession as 'a cancelable right to cash flow' (page 26) granted for a defined period, typically by competitive bid, and BOT as the greenfield version.

WHERE A PFI OR PF2 DEAL SITS

A UK PFI contract is a concession of the availability kind: the project company builds, finances and maintains an asset and is paid a unitary charge by the public body for 25 to 30 years (National Audit Office 2018, paragraph 2, page 4), so, on my reading, revenue risk is not transferred to it, unlike the concession in Guasch's table. This is why the table's revenue-risk row matters: it is the dividing line between a demand-risk concession (a toll road) and an availability PPP (a school).

title: Hart (2003): Bundling Build and Operate
notes:
THE PAPER

Hart, O. (2003), Incomplete contracts and public ownership: remarks, and an application to public-private partnerships, Economic Journal 113(486), C69 to C76; I read the CMPO Working Paper 03/061 (July 2002), whose printed pages are cited here. The second half of the paper, pages 5 to 11, develops what Hart calls a very preliminary model of PPPs.

THE MODEL

Three dates: build between dates 0 and 1, operate between 1 and 2 (page 5). The contract is incomplete, so the builder can make two investments that the contract cannot verify. Investment i is productive, a better, airier, easier-to-run prison that raises the benefit B and lowers the operating cost C. Investment e is unproductive: it reduces cost and quality, 'the quality-shading investment' (page 6), as when the builder installs an electric fence that cuts the number of guards but is not what the government had in mind. The first best sets the marginal social benefit of i equal to its cost, and sets e to zero on Hart's assumption that c'(0) - b'(0) is at most 1 (page 6).

Under conventional provision the builder is paid a fixed price and does not internalise the operating cost, so he chooses i = e = 0 (page 7). Under a PPP he does internalise it, so he chooses i and e such that the marginal cost saving equals the marginal cost of investment (page 8): more of the productive investment, which is still too little because he is not paid for the benefit to society, and more of the unproductive one, which is too much (pages 9 to 10).

THE RULE

'Conventional provision ("unbundling") is good if the quality of the building can be well specified, whereas the quality of the service can't.' A PPP is good if the quality of the service can be specified, or there are good performance measures, whereas the quality of the building can't (page 10). Hart's examples: prisons and schools probably fall in the first category, hospitals in the second (page 10).

HART'S CHALLENGE TO THE FINANCING CASE

Page 11: policy makers often argue that PPPs are good because the private sector is a cheaper source of financing or insurance than the public sector; 'this thinking is strange for an economist', since it is hard to imagine an agent more able to borrow or insure than the government with its powers of taxation. He suggests attention should move from financing to relative contracting costs. The next two models pick up this point.

SOURCE AND CAUTION

CMPO Working Paper 03/061, pages 5 to 11; the Economic Journal pagination differs and I have not seen the published version. The working paper says the model takes contract length as given and abstracts from ownership at the end of the contract (page 11). The paper writes the model for a prison; applying it to a road or a hospital, as the slide does, is Hart's own extension in the examples on page 10.

Model: the builder makes two investments the contract cannot verify: a better building, and corner-cutting that lowers cost and quality Result: bundling gives the builder the operating saving, so he invests more in the building and cuts more corners Rule: conventional provision if the building can be specified and the service cannot; a PPP in the opposite case Hart, O. (2003), Incomplete contracts and public ownership: remarks, and an application to public-private partnerships, Economic Journal 113(486), C69–C76; CMPO Working Paper 03/061, pages 5–11.

title: Bundling and the Limits of the Contract
notes:
INTERACTIVE: web/bundling-build-and-operate.html (button at top right)

THE FIGURE

Net benefit to the government under Hart's model for the four combinations of what each contract can specify. Parameters: psi = 1 (operating saving from a better building), beta = 1 (benefit to society of the same building), gamma = 2 (saving from cutting corners) and delta = 1.5 (quality lost by cutting corners), so gamma - delta = 0.5, within Hart's assumption that shading is never worth doing. The first best is i = 4 and e = 0 for a net benefit of 4. The conventional contract gives zero if the building cannot be specified (the builder chooses i = e = 0) and the first best if it can. The PPP gives 1.5 if the service cannot be specified (i = 1 and e = 1: more building investment, and corner-cutting that destroys value) and 3.0 if it can (i = 1 and e = 0).

HOW THE FIGURE WAS BUILT

The functional forms are mine: psi(i) = 2 Psi sqrt(i), beta(i) = 2 Beta sqrt(i), c(e) = gamma e - e squared over 2 and b(e) = delta e + e squared over 2, chosen so the first-order conditions on pages 6 to 8 of Hart's working paper have closed solutions. The two switches (building specified, service specified) turn Hart's closing argument on page 10 into a calculation: a specified building lets the conventional contract reach the first best, and a specified service lets the PPP penalise corner-cutting. They are free in the model; Hart does not price the cost of writing a contract, and says that relative contracting costs are the central issue (page 11). The numbers are therefore illustrations of the logic and not estimates. The model was computed in Python (models_w2.py) and JavaScript (the page), and the two agree to 14 decimal places on 300 random parameter sets (check_models.py).

WHAT TO TRY ON THE PAGE

Untick both switches and raise beta: the PPP's advantage over conventional provision shrinks relative to the first best, because the benefit of the building is one no builder is paid for. Raise delta to 3 with beta at 0: corner-cutting destroys value and the PPP loses its advantage unless the service can be specified. The two questions at the foot of the page do these.

title: Engel, Fischer and Galetovic (2013): Sharing Demand Risk
notes:
THE PAPER

Engel, E., Fischer, R. and Galetovic, A. (2013), The basic public finance of public-private partnerships, Journal of the European Economic Association 11(1), 83 to 111. I read the NBER Working Paper 13284 (July 2007); page numbers are its printed pages (printed page = PDF page minus two).

SETTING

A government contracts a risk-averse firm to build, operate and maintain an infrastructure project. The investment is upfront; demand is exogenous, stochastic and perfectly inelastic; the firm is paid a mix of state-dependent user fees and subsidies (page 2). The range runs from traditional provision, where the government pays and the firm collects no fees, to a full concession, where fees are the only repayment. A pound raised in tax costs society more than a pound, and a subsidy is a less efficient way of paying the firm than user fees, because the private sector pays lower overhead and is less corrupt and less bureaucratic (pages 3 and 13).

FIRST RESULT

PPPs do not release public funds: private financing reduces the need for current taxes, but the government forgoes user-fee revenue it could have received later, so there is no net gain in discounted value, and subsidies paid under a PPP are future taxes in place of current ones (pages 2 to 3; Table 1, page 41). The paper therefore puts the PPP closer to public provision than to privatisation in terms of the risk profile of the government's budget (page 41). This is the formal version of Hart's remark on financing.

SECOND RESULT: THE OPTIMAL CONTRACT

The optimal risk-sharing contract has a minimum revenue guarantee m and a revenue cap M (Proposition 2, page 15). In low-demand states the concession lasts indefinitely and the firm receives a subsidy that tops revenue up to m. In intermediate states it lasts indefinitely and no subsidy is paid. In high-demand states the firm collects M in present value and the concession ends in finite time, so the term is variable, and the government collects the rest. How far apart m and M are depends on the firm's risk aversion and the inefficiency of subsidies (page 15).

THE PRACTICAL POINT

The authors find that observed revenue guarantees and revenue-sharing arrangements differ from those the optimal contract implies, and that the optimal guarantees and caps bear no relation to the observed ones (pages 2 and 6). They also say that contracts have been renegotiated in favour of the concessionaire in many cases, when demand was lower than expected, citing Guasch (2004) (page 2): the link to part six.

CAUTION

The model is stylised: the investment is upfront, there are no further costs, and the base case has no moral hazard (the paper extends it later; I did not read that section closely). The concession term is the contract variable in the model, so it fits toll roads better than availability PPPs.

title: The Optimal Concession Contract
notes:
INTERACTIVE: web/sharing-demand-risk.html (button at top right)

THE FIGURE

The vertical axis is what the concessionaire receives, in present value, in each state of demand (the horizontal axis is the present value of user fees the project would earn if run indefinitely). The three lines are the contracts compared in the page. The pure concession (green) gives the firm whatever the traffic produces. Conventional provision (dashed) pays the firm the investment of 100 in every state. The optimal contract (brown) is Engel et al.'s Proposition 2 (page 15): flat at the guarantee m for low demand, equal to fees in the middle, flat again at the cap M for high demand. At these inputs m is 83.6 and M is 105.9; the state pays an expected subsidy of 0.9 and takes an expected 20.5 of fees above the cap.

INPUTS

Investment I = 100; demand uniform between 70 and 170; exponential utility with risk aversion 0.01; subsidy waste zeta = 0.25; cost of public funds lambda = 0.3, and alpha (the paper's parameter for the value of public funds) set to zero. The expected social cost, (1 + lambda) times expected revenue collected plus (1 + lambda)(1 + zeta) times expected subsidy, is 130.8 under the optimal contract, 162.5 for conventional provision and 156.0 for the pure concession, which also leaves the firm an expected certainty-equivalent profit of 15.9 that a competitive auction would remove.

HOW IT WAS BUILT

The structure is Engel et al.: the planner's programme on pages 12 to 13 (equations 6a to 6d), the first-order conditions u'(m - I) = (1 + zeta) u'(M - I) and u'(M - I) = ... on page 15, and the three demand states of Proposition 2. The parametrisation is mine: with exponential utility the first-order conditions give M - m = ln(1 + zeta) / rho, and m comes from the firm's zero-profit condition E[u(T - I)] = u(0), which I solve by bisection, with T the firm's total receipts. Demand is uniform so the expectations have closed forms. The model was computed in Python (models_w2.py) and JavaScript (the page) and agrees to 14 decimal places on 300 random parameter sets. This is a teaching illustration of the contract's shape: do not read the cost figures as estimates.

CAUTION

The paper's general result holds for any demand distribution; the uniform choice is only for tractability. The cost ranking depends on lambda and zeta, which the page lets students vary, and the sign of the comparison with the pure concession depends on how much rent the firm keeps.

title: Private Finance and the Public Sector Comparator
notes:
THE FIGURE

The chart redraws the logic of the National Audit Office's Figure 3 (page 14), which shows that repaying £100 over 30 years in equal annual instalments costs £34, £53, £73, £95, £118, £142 and £166 in interest at 2 to 8 per cent. My annuity formula reproduces all seven to within rounding (check in models_w2.py). The bars take five rates: the 2.5 per cent the NAO uses for government borrowing in its comparator (Figure 4, note 2, page 16), and gilts plus the premiums the NAO quotes in paragraph 1.17 (page 14). Interest on £100 over 30 years: 43 at 2.5 per cent, 84 at 4.5, 124 at 6.25, 130 at 6.5 and 166 at 8.

THE FACTS

Paragraph 1.17 (page 14): the 2010 National Infrastructure Plan estimated an indicative cost of capital for PFI of 2 to 3.75 per cent above gilts; data collected by the Infrastructure and Projects Authority on deals since 2013 forecast debt and equity returns 2 to 4 per cent above government borrowing; four social housing deals of 2013 projected over 8 per cent, more than 5 per cent above gilts at the time. Illustration: £100 repaid over 30 years costs £34 in interest at 2 per cent and £73 at 4. Paragraph 1.19 (pages 15 to 16): the Department for Education estimated PF2 costs for one group of schools about 40 per cent higher than a project financed by government borrowing (Figure 4), and the Treasury Committee in 2011 estimated a privately financed hospital at 70 per cent higher. Other costs: lender arrangement fees of about 1 per cent (up to 2), project company costs of 1 to 2 per cent of the payment, insurance, cash held in project companies (more than £4 billion collectively) and advisers (paragraph 1.18, page 15).

THE OTHER SIDE

The Treasury considers that risk transfer can produce benefits that outweigh the higher financing cost (paragraph 1.5, page 8): certainty over construction cost, operating efficiency, better-maintained assets. The NAO finds that cost certainty is generally seen as a benefit (paragraph 1.6, page 9) but that the cost of services in its hospital samples was similar, with no evidence of operational efficiency, and that more recent London data show higher cost of services such as cleaning under PFI (paragraph 1.9, page 10). Some benefits can be obtained with fixed-price contracts without a long-term private finance contract (paragraph 1.8). It takes no view on the value for money of the programme as a whole (paragraph 1 of the Overview).

BUDGET INCENTIVES

Most private-finance debt is off the national accounts balance sheet and does not score upfront against departmental budgets, which gives short-term incentives to use it unrelated to value for money (paragraph 1.14, page 11); five of six departments that could answer said their capital budgets would not have covered the investment otherwise. This is the point Engel et al. make formally: no budget relief in present value.

title: The Saving Needed to Offset Private Finance
notes:
INTERACTIVE: web/price-of-private-finance.html (button at top right)

THE FIGURE

For a £100 project over 30 years, how much of the operating and maintenance cost must the bundled private contract save for the privately financed route to cost the same as the public one in present value? Both cash streams are valued at the gilt yield, which is the government's own cost of funds. The public route repays the £100 as a level annuity at gilts (2.5 per cent) and pays operating cost O, assumed to be 4 per cent of capital a year (£4). The private route borrows the £100 plus a 1 per cent arrangement fee at gilts plus the spread, grosses the payment up by 1.5 per cent for the project company's costs, and pays O less the saving. The saving needed is the extra annual financing payment divided by O: 38 per cent at a spread of 2.0 points, 72 per cent at 3.75 and 108 per cent at 5.5, which is more than the whole operating cost. At the page's default spread of 3.0 the answer is 57 per cent, and the financing premium is worth £47.6 per £100 in present value.

HOW TO READ IT

This is a public sector comparator in the form the NAO describes, stripped to its financing arithmetic. It is a test of Hart's remark and of Engel et al.'s result in numbers: if the government can borrow more cheaply, the private route must earn back the difference through the bundle. The operating cost of 4 per cent of capital is my assumption, flagged on the page: a service-heavy asset such as a hospital has a larger share and so a lower breakeven, a road a smaller one and a higher breakeven, which is the Hart argument in numerical form (bundling pays where operating cost is large and responsive to design).

WHAT IS LEFT OUT

Risk transfer is not priced: the breakeven saving is, in effect, the value of risk transfer plus efficiency that the contract has to deliver. Tax and the timing of repayments are ignored. The comparator rates and fee figures come from the NAO (paragraphs 1.17 and 1.18, and Figure 4, note 2) but the combination is my construction, not an NAO calculation, and the NAO does not report a breakeven. The model was computed in Python and JavaScript and agrees to 14 decimal places on 300 random parameter sets.

THE FIGURE

The bars are the overall score from 1 to 4; the markers are the three dimensions, each weighted equally: policy and political commitment, the legal and regulatory framework, and PPP-supporting arrangements such as dedicated PPP units, standard contracts and green-lighting procedures (pages 26 to 28). title: Three Models of the Contract Compared
notes:
THE TABLE

A comparison of the three models and the framework on what each tries to explain, what it predicts, and how it fares against evidence. It is the synthesis slide of the focus part and, if time is short, the one to keep.

Hart (2003): explains whether build and operate should be bundled. Prediction: bundle when the service can be specified and the building cannot. Evidence: no direct test in the paper; it is a model whose test is the sector pattern (the prison, school and hospital examples, page 10). The practical difficulty is that the question 'can the service be specified?' is itself a judgement.

Engel, Fischer and Galetovic (2013): explains how demand risk should be shared, and what a PPP does to the budget. Predictions: guarantee and cap; no relief to the budget in present value. Evidence: the authors note renegotiation when demand is lower than expected (page 2), and Guasch's data (next part) are consistent with that; observed guarantees differ from the optimum (page 6).

Private finance (National Audit Office 2018): explains what the bundle has to save. Prediction: the financing premium has to be earned back. Evidence: premium of 2 to 4 points over gilts; PF2 schools about 40 per cent dearer than a comparator; no evidence of operational efficiency in hospitals (paragraphs 1.9 and 1.17 to 1.19). The NAO does not form a view on the programme's value for money.

Framework (Verhoest et al. 2015): explains what governments do to support PPPs. Finding: support varies across countries and does not come as a package; the link to uptake is positive but modest (r = 0.31 and 0.58; thesis page 34).

TEACHING POINT

The three models give three different tests of a project: what is each party able to specify; who bears the demand risk and what does the contract do when demand is wrong; what has to be saved to pay for the cost of finance. A project that passes only one of the three should be questioned. Students' group-project reports should say which of the three they rely on.

title: Development Finance Institutions
notes:
THE ARGUMENT

Multilateral development banks (MDBs) lend directly and, the claim goes, mobilise private lenders. Broccolini, Lotti, Maffioli, Presbitero and Stucchi (2019), Mobilization Effects of Multilateral Development Banks, IDB Invest (Inter-American Investment Corporation) Development through the Private Sector Series, Technical Note 16, March 2019, test the claim using loan-level data on syndicated lending to a large sample of developing countries from 1993 to 2017.

THE POINTS ON THE SLIDE

Scale (page 1): the United Nations estimates achieving the Sustainable Development Goals needs investment up to USD 3.9 trillion a year; at current levels the annual investment gap in developing countries is about USD 2.5 trillion (UNCTAD 2014); official development assistance was USD 143 billion in 2016, an order of magnitude smaller than the need. MDB loan capacity is small relative to needs, so MDBs have pledged to catalyse private investment (page 1).

Two channels (page 14): signalling and demonstration, since MDB private-sector windows lend on commercial terms and their lending signals good opportunities, and may encourage government reform; and risk mitigation and better information, since MDBs can extend preferred creditor status (their loans have been excluded from sovereign debt reschedulings), keep close relationships with countries and monitor projects, which fills information gaps and mitigates political risk for private lenders.

Example (page 1): the Panama Canal expansion, financed by the IDB Group, three other multilaterals and the Japan Bank for International Cooperation, amounted to 30 per cent of GDP and in the five years after its announcement is estimated to have raised almost USD 9.9 billion in private investment, 1.8 times the project cost (Lanzalot et al. 2018, as cited; not read).

CAUTION

The note is a working paper by staff of an MDB group, and the authors are the institution's own economists; read the findings with that in mind. The peer-reviewed version appeared later (I believe World Bank Economic Review, 2021; check before citing). Preferred creditor treatment is described, not tested, in the passages I used.

SOURCE

Broccolini et al. (2019), IDB Invest Technical Note 16, pages 1 and 14 (printed pages; PDF page minus three), under a CC-IGO licence.

(2019), Mobilization Effects of Multilateral Development Banks, IDB Invest Technical Note 16, pages 1 and 14.

title: Mobilisation Effects of Multilateral Lenders
notes:
THE FIGURE

Table 3 of the paper (printed page 30): the cumulative effect of an MDB lending in a country-sector in year t, t-1 and t-2 on four outcomes, estimated with sector-country, sector-year and country-year fixed effects on 24,219 country-sector-years. The grey bars are the sample averages and the brown bars the cumulative effects: the number of syndicated loans per country-sector-year, average 0.760, effect +2.448 (significant only at the 10 per cent level, Wald p = 0.084); loan size as a share of GDP, average 0.105, effect +0.158 (p = 0.003); banks per loan, average 1.526, effect +1.975 (p = 0.002); maturity, average 0.755 years, effect +0.790 years (p below 0.001). Averages and effects are from the table's rows 'Average' and 'Wald test'.

THE FINDINGS

Abstract: positive and significant direct and indirect mobilisation effects on the number of deals and the size of bank inflows; the number of lenders and the average maturity of syndicated loans also increase; effects last up to three years and are not offset by a decline in bond financing; there is no evidence of anticipation effects (Table 4, page 31, where the coefficients on future MDB presence are insignificant) and the results are not driven by large global banks (Table 5, page 32), Chinese lending or aid flows.

READING THE SIZE

The effects are large relative to the averages, because the averages are low: most country-sector-years have no syndicated loan. The coefficients are not an elasticity and the estimates do not say what share of private lending would have happened anyway: they are differences between country-sectors with and without an MDB loan in the previous three years, conditional on the fixed effects. The note says the effects are sizeable and suggests MDBs can play a vital role in mobilising private finance, which is the authors' conclusion, not mine.

CAUTION

The sample is syndicated bank lending to developing countries; infrastructure is one of several sectors, so the note's findings are not specific to infrastructure projects. I did not read the extensions that split the sample by sector.

Broccolini et al. (2019), IDB Invest Technical Note 16, abstract and Tables 3 to 5 (printed pages 30 to 32).

title: Concessions and Renegotiation
notes:
THE FIGURE

Guasch (2004), Table 1.7, printed page 13: the share of concessions renegotiated, in a dataset of more than 1,000 concessions granted in Latin America and the Caribbean from 1985 to 2000. All concessions 30 per cent; excluding telecommunications (almost all privatised and not conceded), 41.5; electricity 9.7; transportation 54.7; water and sanitation 74.4 (pages 12 to 13).

THE POINTS

Renegotiation is most common in water and sanitation, and in transport, and far less common in telecommunications and energy, which Guasch attributes to the more competitive nature of those sectors, reducing the concessionaire's leverage: the government has other suppliers to turn to if the operator threatens to leave (page 13). Timing: the average time from award to renegotiation was 2.2 years, with water and sanitation quickest at 1.6 years and transport 3.1 (Table 1.8, page 14), for concessions meant to run 15 to 30 years; 85 per cent of renegotiations occurred within four years of award and 60 per cent within three (Table 1.9, page 14). On average the outcome of renegotiation adversely affected users (page 12), and a Latinobarometro survey of 2001 found 63 per cent of people in 17 countries thought privatisation had not been beneficial, up from 43 per cent in 1998 (page 12).

DEFINITION

Renegotiation here means a significant change in a concession contract not envisioned or driven by stated contingencies, covering tariffs, investment plans, exclusivity, guarantees, lump-sum payments or fees, coverage targets, service standards or the concession period. Standard scheduled tariff adjustments and periodic reviews are not counted (page 12).

CAUTION

The sample is Latin America and the Caribbean in the 1990s, a period of rapid privatisation after macroeconomic crises; it would be a mistake to generalise to the UK PFI. UK PFI contracts have been modified too (the NAO notes capital cost increases in PFI housing, paragraph 1.6, page 9), but I do not have a comparable dataset.

SOURCE

Guasch, J. L. (2004), Granting and Renegotiating Infrastructure Concessions: Doing It Right, World Bank Institute, Tables 1.7 to 1.9 (pages 13 to 14); printed page = PDF page minus 16 in the copy I used.

title: Contract Features and Renegotiation
notes:
THE FIGURE

Guasch (2004), Table 1.16 (printed page 17) and Table 1.11 (page 15): the incidence of renegotiation by award criterion, by what the contract regulates, and by how the concession was awarded. Awarded on the lowest tariff, 60 per cent renegotiated; on the highest transfer fee, 11. Contracts with investment requirements ('regulation by means'), 70; with performance indicators ('regulation by objectives'), 18. Awarded by competitive bidding, 46 per cent (excluding telecommunications); by bilateral negotiation, 8. These are tabulations, not estimates with controls.

THE EXPLANATIONS

Guasch (page 15): bilateral negotiation lets the operator extract much more favourable concession terms and that flexibility lessens the incentive to renegotiate later. By implication, competitive bidding on the lowest tariff encourages aggressive bids that cannot be sustained, which are then reopened: this is the winner's-curse reading, and it is Guasch's and the wider literature's, not an inference from the table. Investment obligations lock the operator into a schedule that changes in demand or cost can make unattainable, which performance indicators avoid (page 16). Most concessions, 73 per cent, had investment obligations; 21 per cent had performance indicators only; 6 per cent both (Table 1.15, page 17).

THE LESSON

The competition for the market that Joskow (pages 64 to 66) describes as a substitute for regulation works only if the contract that results is complete enough to stand: competition at the award stage buys a low price today, and a contract that is later reopened. A bid on the highest transfer fee, with performance indicators and not input requirements, was least likely to be reopened.

CAUTION

The comparison between competitive and bilateral awards excludes telecommunications, and the award criterion is correlated with sector and with the macroeconomic setting, so the figures are associations only. I did not read the book's later chapters on the determinants.

title: Initiators of Renegotiation
notes:
THE FIGURE

Guasch (2004), Table 1.14, printed page 16: who initiated the renegotiation, in per cent of requests, by regulatory regime. Price cap: operator 83, both 11, government 6. Hybrid regime: operator 44, both 30, government 26. Rate of return: operator 26, both 39, government 34 (these three add to 99 in the table, by rounding). Across all concessions, operators initiated 61 per cent of renegotiations and governments 26, with the rest joint (Table 1.13, page 16).

THE EXPLANATION

Guasch, page 16: under rate-of-return regulation the government led the requests, although with a much lower incidence; the operator's dominance under a price cap is partly explained by the increased risk to the operator of that regime. Note the mechanism this implies: a price cap passes demand and cost risk to the operator, and when risk materialises, the operator is the one who asks to reopen the contract.

LINK TO THE ENGEL, FISCHER AND GALETOVIC MODEL

Engel et al. (page 2) explain renegotiation in favour of the concessionaire as the result of contracts that did not take proper account of demand risk: renegotiations take place when demand is lower than expected, and the array of risk-sharing agreements in practice follows from the same cause. Their design response is the contract on the optimal-concession slide: write the sharing of demand risk in advance, as a guarantee and a cap, in place of negotiating afterwards. This is a proposition about design and not a finding of the renegotiation data, which do not record demand outcomes.

LINK TO THE CASE

The Heathrow case that follows shows the other side of a long relationship between a state and a private partner: how the state plans, consents and regulates a project it does not own.

title: Case Study: Heathrow Airport Expansion (Hannah Newell, DfT)
notes:
AN OUTLINE ONLY

By Helen's instruction this is one slide, naming the ground the case covers and leaving the discussion to Hannah Newell, Director, Heathrow Expansion, Department for Transport. It states no facts about the case, takes no position and makes no claims, so it cannot spoil what she says.

THE FOUR HEADINGS

The headings follow the angle Hannah proposed in her own words, 'planning nationally significant infrastructure in the UK, meaning Heathrow, and the relationship between state and private partners developing this' (email thread of June and July 2026, recorded in Admin/Guest speakers/Hannah Newell - DfT - Week 2 government and regulators.md): planning a nationally significant infrastructure project; the relationship between the state and its private partners; stakeholders and the governance of a contested project; and a discussion with the guest.

HOW THE WEEK PREPARES THE CASE

The role of the state and the commitment problem (part 1 and slide 10) frame why a state and a regulated private airport owner must keep a relationship that neither can exit cheaply. Regulation of natural monopoly (part 3) supplies the vocabulary for the airport's economic regulation. The delivery models (part 4) supply three questions to put to any project: what can the contract specify, who bears demand risk, and what does the financing cost. The renegotiation evidence (part 6) supplies the question of what happens to a deal when conditions change. Students should leave the theory hour with those questions in hand, and Hannah's session is where they are put to a real project.

title: Summary
notes:
The same list as the Lecture Outline at the start of the deck, under a different title, as in the RE02 decks and the Week 1 deck. There is no thank-you slide (Helen's rule, 2026-10-25): the summary is the last slide.

Run back through it one sentence per item. The state is involved because of natural monopoly, sunk costs, incomplete contracts and asymmetric information. Public investment management is the set of institutions that choose projects, and their appraisal and evaluation stages are the weak ones. Regulation of a natural monopoly trades information against incentive, and is exposed to capture, ratchets and hold-up. A PPP can be understood as a bundle of tasks (Hart), a sharing of demand risk (Engel, Fischer and Galetovic) or a way of raising finance whose premium has to be earned back (National Audit Office). Multilateral banks mobilise private lenders and the effect is large relative to the average. Concessions are renegotiated often, and soon, and more often where they were competitively bid on the lowest tariff or loaded with investment obligations. The case is where all of this meets a real project.
